Global Fuel Price Trends & Policy Impact Analysis (2020–2026)

A trend and policy-impact analysis of weekly retail fuel prices across 84 countries (Jan 2020–Apr 2026), benchmarking retail petrol/diesel/LPG (USD/L) against Brent Crude (USD/bbl) and national fiscal settings (tax share, subsidy regime).
Coverage: 2020-01-06 → 2026-04-06 (327 weeks) Rows: 27,468 Regions: 7 Audience: Policy analysts

4) Impact of Subsidies and Taxation on Retail Prices

Price level buffering: In this dataset, countries with higher subsidy labels (“Medium/High/Very High”, binned as High) exhibit substantially lower mean retail fuel prices than Low-subsidy countries.
  • Mean petrol: High-subsidy 0.996 vs Low-subsidy 3.451 USD/L (dampening 71.1%)
  • Mean diesel: High-subsidy 0.912 vs Low-subsidy 3.244 USD/L (dampening 71.9%)
Pass-through slope by subsidy bin (weekly averages):
  • High-subsidy: petrol ≈ -0.0014 + 0.00935 × brent
  • Low-subsidy: petrol ≈ -0.0009 + 0.03235 × brent
Interpretation: the high-subsidy bin shows a smaller USD/L per USD/bbl slope, consistent with stronger buffering of crude moves in price levels.
High-subsidy countries maintain lower price levels across the full horizon.
Scatter uses sampled points; tax share is an estimated percentage of retail price.

6) Key Findings & Policy Implications

Key findings (data-derived):
  1. Weekly Brent–retail co-movement is extremely tight at the global level: Pearson r = 0.996 for weekly % changes in Brent vs average petrol (diesel: r = 0.995).
  2. The largest volatility episode in this dataset occurs in 2020: Brent weekly % change volatility (std) peaks at 0.0272 (petrol peaks at 0.0273).
  3. Across all observations, high-subsidy countries (binning Medium/High/Very High as 'High') show materially lower average retail prices: petrol dampening = 71.1% vs low-subsidy; diesel dampening = 71.9%.
  4. Regional inequality widens over time: the regional petrol spread (max–min) is 2.870 USD/L in 2026, with 2020–2026 showing an overall upward drift in spreads.
  5. Tax share differs by income group: average tax_percentage is 34.72% (High income) vs 21.11% (Middle) vs 22.86% (Low).
Policy implications (actionable):
  • Treat subsidy design as a volatility-management instrument: ensure automatic, rules-based mechanisms (e.g., sliding excise or stabilization funds) to avoid ad-hoc adjustments.
  • Target support rather than universal price suppression: broad subsidies reduce average prices but can be fiscally expensive; prioritize vulnerable households or essential transport sectors.
  • Recalibrate tax structures for stability: consider shifting from ad-valorem components to specific taxes or bands to reduce amplification when crude rises sharply.
  • Improve transparency of price components: publish clear decompositions (crude, refining, distribution, tax, subsidy) to strengthen accountability and reduce policy uncertainty.
Recommendations are framed to be implementation-agnostic; adapt to local fiscal constraints and distributional goals.

Data integrity notes & limitations

  • The dataset documentation describes subsidy_level as High/Low, but observed values include Medium and Very High. This report bins Medium/High/Very High as “High” for segmentation to avoid data loss.
  • tax_percentage varies week-to-week within countries; treat it as an estimate rather than a static statutory rate.
  • Brent is global per week; correlations at the global-average level can appear near-1 in levels. The report therefore emphasizes correlations on weekly % changes for pass-through dynamics.
